Heuer is a Swiss watch and stopwatch maker, founded by Edouard Heuer in Saint-Imier in 1860 and
known since 1985 as TAG Heuer.[^wiki] Its mechanical split-second timers were sold to American
swim coaches and officials through the 1960s. In 1973 it introduced the Microsplit, one of the
first quartz digital stopwatches advertised to swimmers.[^sw6305][^sw7309] From 1973 until shortly
after the 1980 Winter Olympics, Heuer was a member of [Swiss Timing](swiss-timing.md), the joint
sports-timing company of the Swiss watch industry.[^donze][^sthistory]

## History

This section follows the company through its stopwatch business and its part in Olympic timing.

### Mechanical timers

Heuer built precision stopwatches from early in the twentieth century. Its Mikrograph of 1916
measured to 1/100 s, and Heuer timed the three Summer Olympics of the 1920s.[^wiki][^museum] In
the 1960s the company joined with Leonidas and traded as Heuer-Leonidas.[^wiki] In the United
States, stopwatch dealers listed Heuer timers in Swimming World from 1960. The model most often
advertised was the No. 572, a tenth-second split-action timer with a 30-minute register that
dealers called the "Olympic timer". It cost $74.50 in 1963.[^sw6005][^sw6305] In 1968, the year of
the Mexico City Games, its advertising carried the line "Olympic time is Heuer time".[^sw6807] By
1971 Heuer sold its stopwatches in the United States through Heuer Time & Electronics Corporation of
Springfield, New Jersey. The company then claimed more than 100 models built on one movement
family, the caliber 7700.[^sw7103]

### Microsplit

Heuer's first digital stopwatches appeared in Swimming World in September 1973 under the
Microsplit name. The advertisement compared three models: the HL 802 reading to tenths of a
second, the HL 813 reading to hundredths of a minute, and the HL 820 reading to hundredths of a
second. All three were quartz-controlled, ran on four AA mercury cells and had a sunshade over the
LED display. Only the HL 820 had a split-split function and an input for automatic starting and
stopping.[^sw7309] A dealer's list of December 1973 prices an "HL 800" with tenths alongside the HL
820, a model number the maker's own table does not use.[^sw7312] TAG Heuer now dates the first
Microsplit, the 800, to 1972 and calls it the first digital stopwatch. [Accusplit](accusplit.md)
makes the same claim for its own 1972 model.[^tagdigital]

A smaller LED model, the 530, followed in 1975, advertised as the smallest digital stopwatch made.
It weighed 4 ounces and timed in split, Taylor lap and split-split modes.[^sw7505] A
liquid-crystal Microsplit, readable in sunlight and listed at $85, followed in 1976.[^sw7610] A
1976 Microsplit designed by Richard Sapper is reported to be in the design collection of the
Museum of Modern Art.[^sapper]

### Swiss Timing

Swiss Timing was founded in 1972 by the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, Omega and
Longines, and Heuer joined it in 1973.[^sthistory][^donze] At the 1976 Games in Montreal and
Innsbruck, the company's partner brands were Omega, Longines and Heuer.[^sthistory] Heuer was
official timekeeper of the 1980 Winter Olympics at Lake Placid, and a stopwatch dealer advertised
the Microsplit 230 in 1979 with the line "Official timer of the 1980
Olympics".[^donze][^sw7901] Heuer
left Swiss Timing soon after Lake Placid.[^donze] A 1985 product notice calls Heuer the official
timekeeper of "the 1980 Olympic Games" without naming them. Some secondary accounts also place
Heuer at the Moscow Summer Games that year, but no source found here confirms that.[^st8505]

### Later stopwatches

In the early 1980s Heuer Time & Electronics sold the 1000 series of Microsplits, which started at
$39.95. They included the water-protected 1020, advertised as suited to swimming, and the
water-resistant 1030 with lap and cumulative split modes.[^sw8112][^st8205] Double-display
Microsplits with a countdown timer followed in 1985.[^sw8511] In 1985 the company became TAG
Heuer, and in 1986 Swimming World carried TAG-Heuer advertisements claiming more than 180 kinds of
stopwatch.[^wiki][^sw8612] No later Heuer stopwatch advertising to swimmers was found. LVMH
bought the company in 1999.[^wiki]

This section lists the timers advertised to swimmers, in the order they appeared. Prices are as

|---|---|---|
| #33.206 | 1960 | Mechanical; 1/10 s; 7 jewels; $28.50[^sw6005] |
| No. 572 | 1963 or earlier | Mechanical 1/10 s split-action timer; 15 jewels; 30-minute register; $74.50[^sw6305] |
| Microsplit HL 802, HL 813, HL 820 | September 1973 | Quartz; LED; four AA cells; HL 820 with split-split and automatic start/stop input; $190–220[^sw7309] |
| Microsplit 530 | May 1975 | Smaller LED model; 4 oz; split, Taylor and split-split; $149.50 from a dealer[^sw7505][^sw7510] |
| HL-420, HL-430 | 1976 | Dealer prices $109.90 and $79.95[^sw7605] |
| LCD Microsplit | 1976 | Liquid crystal display; to 59:59.99; split and time-out; $85[^sw7610] |
| Microsplit 230, 235 | 1978 | Round LCD; split (230) or lap (235); fail-safe reset; $69.95[^sw7809][^sw7901] |
| 1000 series (1000, 1010, 1020, 1030) | 1981 | From $39.95; 1020 water-protected; 1030 lap or cumulative split[^sw8112][^st8205] |
| Double-display Microsplits (1015, 1035) | 1985 | Countdown plus stopwatch on two displays; 1035 with split, lap and lap count[^sw8511] |

## In swim timing

Heuer timers were sold for the manual side of swim timing. In the 1960s dealers offered them for
official AAU timing, and in 1966 one sold three Heuer timers together with a Minerva
tri-timer board.[^sw6404][^sw6603] The digital Microsplits were advertised for
swimming among other sports, and Heuer described the water-protected Microsplit 1020 of 1981 as
suited to swimming events.[^sw7505][^sw8112] In Canada the Quebec swimming federation offered
electronic Heuer and Seiko stopwatches to its clubs in 1977.[^sn7706]

Heuer reached swimmers through several distributors. In 1973–1975 the Microsplit was handled by
regional agents in California, Michigan and New Jersey. Heuer Time & Electronics then advertised
under its own name from 1976, and [Seagull Enterprises](seagull.md) distributed Heuer stopwatches
in 1977 and 1978.[^sw7309][^sw7505][^sw7610][^sn7808] Its rivals in the digital stopwatch market
included [Accusplit](accusplit.md), [Cronus](cronus.md) and [Siliconix](siliconix.md).[^sw7503]
